\section*{Score-I papers}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P1-PHY-S2-Q08, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=1, qno=8, type=multi, subtopic={Satellites}, answer={A,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: orbit, two equal masses given tangential speeds | steps: centre of mass frame; angular momentum and energy conservation; circular if speed equals sqrt(G m / (2 l)); elliptical otherwise; check | I: two body problem reduced to one body}]
Two equal masses $m$ are at a distance $\ell$ apart and interact via gravity. They are given proper tangential speed $v_0$, so that they both travel in a circular of radius $\dfrac{\ell}{2}$ around their CM. If one of the masses is grabbed and held at rest, then the closest distance the other mass comes to it is $r$. Then :
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$v_0=\sqrt{\dfrac{Gm}{2\ell}}$}
\opt{B}{$v_0=\sqrt{\dfrac{Gm}{\ell}}$}
\opt{C}{$r=\dfrac{\ell}{3}$}
\opt{D}{$r=3\ell$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P2-PHY-S1-Q05, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=2, qno=5, type=single, subtopic={Kepler's laws}, answer={C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: speed at an intermediate point, an elliptical planetary orbit | steps: angular momentum and energy conservation between perihelion and aphelion; semi major axis; compute asked speed | I: elliptical orbit constants from extreme distances}]
A planet of small mass $m$ moves around sun of mass $M$ along an elliptical orbit such that its minimum and maximum distance from sun are $r$ and $R$ respectively. Its period of revolution will be
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{(r+R)^2}{6GM}}$}
\opt{B}{$2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{(r+R)^3}{3GM}}$}
\opt{C}{$\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{(r+R)^3}{2GM}}$}
\opt{D}{$2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{(r+R)^3}{GM}}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI03-P1-PHY-S1-Q04, source={Score-I - Test 03 (07 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=4, type=multi, subtopic={Kepler's laws}, answer={A,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K1 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: speed and angular momentum on the elliptical orbit of a spacecraft | steps: perigee and apogee distances give semi major axis; speeds from angular momentum and energy conservation; period from Kepler; check | I: elliptical orbit constants from perigee and apogee}]
In Yuri Gagarin's first manned space flight in 1961, orbit was a closed orbit around Earth. The perigee and apogee were 181 km and 327 km above the Earth. Radius of Earth is 6400 km and $g=10\ \mathrm{ms^{-2}}$ at earth surface. Choose the CORRECT statement(s).
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Time period of orbit was around 5326 seconds}
\opt{B}{Time period of orbit was around 3400 seconds}
\opt{C}{Maximum speed in orbit was around $\dfrac{8\,\mathrm{km}}{\mathrm{sec}}$}
\opt{D}{Semi-major axis of orbit was 6654 km}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI03-P2-PHY-S1-Q08, source={Score-I - Test 03 (07 Jan 2022)}, paper=2, qno=8, type=single, subtopic={Field and potential}, answer={B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=3, diff_parts={K1 S1 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: height at which g decreases by 36 percent | steps: g' = 0.64 g so R/(R + h) = 0.8; h = R/4}]

\begin{qoptions}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI03-P2-PHY-S1-Q09, source={Score-I - Test 03 (07 Jan 2022)}, paper=2, qno=9, type=single, subtopic={Kepler's laws}, answer={D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: satellite, elliptical orbit speed or energy at a point | steps: angular momentum and energy conservation; semi major axis; speed at the extremities; evaluate | I: planet at a focus so orbital elements are needed}]
A satellite of mass $m_0$ is moving in an elliptical orbit around a planet of mass $M$. Planet is fixed at one of the foci of elliptical orbit. The eccentricity of elliptical orbit is $e$. Points A and B are called perihelion and aphelion respectively. The ratio of radius of curvature of elliptical orbit at perihelion to aphelion is
\bfig{80.6}{SI03_p2_phy_s1_q09_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$e$}
\opt{B}{$\dfrac{1-e}{1+e}$}
\opt{C}{$\dfrac1e$}
\opt{D}{$1$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI03-P2-PHY-S2-Q09, source={Score-I - Test 03 (07 Jan 2022)}, paper=2, qno=9, type=numerical, subtopic={Escape velocity}, answer={8.00}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: escape or orbit speed, a spaceship near a planet | steps: energy conservation from hanging motionless to the surface; speed on reaching; or minimum speed to escape; evaluate}]
A spaceship is sent to investigate a planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$. While hanging motionless in space at a distance $5R$ from the centre of the planet, the spaceship fires an instrument package with speed $v_0$ as shown in the figure. The package has mass $m$, which is much smaller than the mass of the spaceship. The angle $\theta$ for which the package just grazes the surface of the planet is $\sin^{-1}\left[\dfrac15\sqrt{1+\dfrac{kGM}{5v_0^2R}}\right]$. Find the value of $k$.
\bfig{129.3}{SI03_p2_phy_s2_q09_1.png}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankpassage}[id=SI08-P1-PHY-S3-G1-2, source={Score-I - Test 08 (09 Feb 2022)}, questions={1-2}]
Recently there has been a lot of hue and cry over the possibility of an asteroid hitting the earth. \begin{bankq}[id=SI17-P1-PHY-S2-Q08, source={Score-I - Test 17 (17 Apr 2022)}, paper=1, qno=8, type=multi, subtopic={Satellites}, answer={B,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=3, diff_parts={K1 S1 I1 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: apparent weight in orbiting satellites at two radii | steps: body in orbit is in free fall so spring reading zero in both orbits; W1 equals W2 equals zero}]

\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$W_1=W_2$}
\opt{B}{$W_1<W_2$}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI17-P2-PHY-S2-Q05, source={Score-I - Test 17 (17 Apr 2022)}, paper=2, qno=5, type=numerical, subtopic={Satellites}, answer={19.8}, answer_src=solved, working={In the uniform asteroid the rock oscillates with omega = 2 pi/15 min; entering at the surface with orbital speed gives amplitude sqrt2 R and the tunnel crossing takes T/4; outside it goes radially up to 2R and returns, taking (pi + 2)/omega; total (2 pi + 2)/omega = T (1 + 1/pi) = 19.8 min. The printed key has no row for this decimal-answer section.}, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: return time, a rock launched into a tunnel through an asteroid | steps: uniform density gives SHM inside with same omega as orbit; entry speed equals orbital speed so amplitude sqrt2 R; outside radial Kepler motion to 2R; add times}]
An alien spaceship is revolving around a spherical asteroid in a very low circular orbit. The period of revolutions of the satellite is 15.0 minutes. A research party of the alien students lands on the asteroid and drills a tunnel through it along the diameter. They then launch a rock into the tunnel with the initial speed equal to that of the orbiting spaceship. How long (in minutes) would it be before the rock comes back to the launch point?
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SII02-P2-PHY-S3-Q03, source={Score-II - Test 02 (28 Mar 2021)}, paper=2, qno=3, type=numerical, subtopic={Field and potential}, answer={3.00}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: three equal masses at the corners of a triangle in circular motion | steps: gravitational force toward the centre from two neighbours; centripetal condition; speed; relative velocity}]
3 identical point particles of mass M move in such a way that distance between particles is `d' which remain constant. Only force is the gravitational force between particles. Then magnitude of relative velocity (in m/s) of one particle with respect to other particle will be:
\[\left[\text{Take}\ \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{d}}=\sqrt3\ \text{m/s}\right]\]
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SII03-P1-PHY-S1-Q14, source={Score-II - Test 03 (05 May 2021)}, paper=1, qno=14, type=single, subtopic={Kepler's laws}, answer={C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K1 S3 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: projectile fired with orbital speed at a general angle | steps: speed sqrt(GM/r) with arbitrary angle; angular momentum and energy conservation; total energy negative; orbit is an ellipse; semi major axis from energy a = r; closest and farthest distances | I: the speed equals circular orbital speed so the semi major axis equals r for any angle}]

\begin{bankq}[id=SII08-P1-PHY-S3-Q01, source={Score-II - Test 08 (05 Feb 2023)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=numerical, subtopic={Kepler's laws}, answer={7.66 to 7.67}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K1 S3 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: escape speed of stars after mass transfer | steps: masses and radii from the density relations; new mass of A after halving the radius at fixed density; thick shell on B with density rho_A; new radius of B; escape speed ratio}]
Two spherical stars $A$ and $B$ have densities $\rho_A$ and $\rho_B$, respectively. Their radius $R_A$ and $R_B$ are related as $5R_A^3 = 2R_B^3$ and their masses $M_A$ and $M_B$ are related by $M_B = 2M_A$. Due to an interaction process, star $A$ loses some of its mass, so that its radius is halved, while its spherical shape is retained, and its density remains $\rho_A$. The entire mass lost by $A$ is deposited as a thick spherical shell on $B$ with the density of the shell being $\rho_A$. If $v_A$ and $v_B$ are the escape velocities from $A$ and $B$ after the interaction process, the ratio $\dfrac{v_B}{v_A} = \sqrt{n}$. The value of $n$ is\_\_\_\_\_\_\_
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SII09-P2-PHY-S3-Q02, source={Score-II - Test 09 (12 Feb 2023)}, paper=2, qno=2, type=numerical, subtopic={Escape velocity}, answer={8}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: gravitational scattering with an impact parameter | steps: energy and angular momentum conservation; hyperbolic orbit; deviation angle formula with the impact parameter; given numbers}]

In one asteroid a tunnel of very small size of depth R is bored to the centre and in other asteroid a spherical cavity of radius $\dfrac{\mathrm R}2$ is made as shown in the figure. Now, identical particles of mass m are dropped into cavities of both asteroids from top most point P. The force experienced by particles are F$_\mathrm I$ and F$_\mathrm{II}$ respectively in cavities of asteroid I and II, when they are x distance away from centre of asteroids. If the time taken by particles to reach the centre of asteroids is T$_\mathrm I$ and T$_\mathrm{II}$ respectively then\par
\bfig{153.0}{SA30_p2_phy_s1_q04_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The ratio of F$_\mathrm I$/F$_\mathrm{II}$ is equal to 2x/R.}
\opt{B}{The ratio of F$_\mathrm I$/F$_\mathrm{II}$ is equal to x/R.}
\opt{C}{The ratio of T$_\mathrm I$/T$_\mathrm{II}$ is equal to $\pi$/4.}
\opt{D}{The ratio of T$_\mathrm I$/T$_\mathrm{II}$ is equal to $\pi$/2.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

The escape velocity from Earth's gravitational field is v$_\mathrm e$ = 11.2 kms$^{-1}$. The minimum initial velocity (v$_\mathrm s$) (in km/sec) required for the rocket to be able to leave the Sun-Earth system is closest to :- (Ignore the rotation and revolution of the Earth and the presence of any other planet)
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SA32-P2-PHY-S1-Q01, source={Score Advanced - Test 32 (08 May 2024)}, paper=2, qno=1, type=single, subtopic={Field and potential}, answer={A}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: small mass passing through a hole in a disk, a hole in it: oscillation along the axis | steps: field on axis of a disk with hole by superposition of disk minus smaller disk; for small displacement near the plane force is linear with height; frequency of small oscillation; period | I: field of a disk on its axis near the plane is linear in height}]
A small block of mass m lies above a thin disk of total mass M, constant surface density $\sigma$, and radius R. A hole of radius R/2 is cut into the center of the disk, allowing the mass to pass though. The mass starts at a position along the central axis of the disk but is displaced a height $\Delta$h from the plane of the disk, where $\Delta$h $<<$ R. There are no other external forces at work on this system; i.e., the disk and block are out in deep space. Assume m $<<$ M. For the first order in $\Delta$h the block undergoes simple harmonic motion with respect to the centre of the plane of the disk, compute the period of oscillation of block.\par
\bfig{119.3}{SA32_p2_phy_s1_q01_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$T=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\pi R}{G\sigma}}$}
\opt{B}{$T=\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi R}{G\sigma}}$}
\opt{C}{$T=\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi R}{2G\sigma}}$}
\opt{D}{None of these}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA33-P2-PHY-S2-Q07, source={Score Advanced - Test 33 (12 May 2024)}, paper=2, qno=7, type=multi, subtopic={Satellites}, answer={A,B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: energy to place a satellite into orbit at 2R, shift it to 3R | steps: energy to launch to circular orbit at r: GM m/R - GMm/(2r) = (3/4) mgR for r = 2R; extra energy to move to 3R: GMm/2 (1/2R - 1/3R) = mgR/12; check options | I: total energy of a circular orbit is minus half the potential}, also_in={Score Advanced - Test 34 (12 May 2024) P2 Q7}]
A sky lab of mass m is first launched from the surface of earth (radius R) in a circular orbit of radius 2R (from centre of earth) and then it is shifted from this circular orbit to another circular orbit of radius 3R.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Minimum energy required to place the lab in first orbit is equal to $\dfrac34$ mgR.}
\opt{B}{Minimum energy required to shift the lab from first orbit to second orbit is $\dfrac{mgR}{12}$.}
\opt{C}{Energy of sky lab in second orbit is greater than its energy in first orbit.}
\opt{D}{Energy of sky lab in second orbit is less than its energy in first orbit.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA34-P1-PHY-S3-Q06, source={Score Advanced - Test 34 (12 May 2024)}, paper=1, qno=6, type=numerical, subtopic={Field and potential}, answer={2.00}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S3 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: spherical cloud expanding after an explosion: speed, escape condition | steps: gravitational potential energy at the surface of a uniform cloud -GM m/R0; kinetic energy at the surface; energy conservation for particles on the surface; total energy sign decides whether the cloud expands forever; maximum radius or velocity at a later radius}, also_in={Score Advanced - Test 36 (19 May 2024) P1 Q6}]
Consider a spherical homogeneous cloud of mass M made by an explosion. Due to energy received from the explosion, it is expanding and the expansion is spherically symmetric. At an instant its radius is R$_0$ and the particles on the surface are moving away from its center with velocity V$_0$. Its radius when expansion ceases is given by\par $\dfrac{nGMR_0}{2GM-R_0V_0^2}$. Find n.
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SA38-P2-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score Advanced - Test 38 (13 Apr 2025)}, paper=2, qno=2, type=single, subtopic={Field and potential}, answer={D}, answer_src=solved, working={Extra potential m alpha/r\^{}3 gives an outward force 3 m alpha/r\^{}4. Centripetal condition: GMm/r0\^{}2 - 3 m alpha/r0\^{}4 = m omega1\^{}2 r0, so omega1\^{}2 = GM/r0\^{}3 - 3 alpha/r0\^{}5. Then (T1\^{}2-T0\^{}2)/T1\^{}2 = 1 - omega1\^{}2/omega0\^{}2 = 3 alpha/(GM r0\^{}2), option D.}, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: change, orbital period under an added 1/r^3 potential at the same radius | steps: original: m r0 omega0^2 = G M m/r0^2; with extra potential m alpha/r^3 force 3 m alpha/r^4 radial inward; new omega^2 = GM/r0^3 + 3 alpha/r0^5; ratio of periods T/T0 = (1 + 3 alpha/(G M r0^2))^{-1/2} | I: derivative of the added potential gives an extra attractive force}]
A particle of mass \textit m is under the influence of the gravitational field of a body of mass \textit M ($\gg$ \textit m). The particle is moving in a circular orbit of radius \textit r$_0$ with time period \textit T$_0$ around the mass \textit M. Then, the particle is subjected to an additional central force, corresponding to the potential energy \textit V$_c$(\textit r) = \textit m$\alpha$/\textit r$^3$, where $\alpha$ is a positive constant of suitable dimensions and \textit r is the distance from the center of the orbit. If the particle moves in the same circular orbit of radius \textit r$_0$ in the combined gravitational potential due to \textit M and \textit V$_c$, but with a new time period \textit T$_1$, then $\dfrac{\mathrm T_1^2-\mathrm T_0^2}{\mathrm T_1^2}$ is given by :- [\textit G is the gravitational constant]
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\dfrac{\alpha}{2\mathrm{GMr}_0^2}$}
\opt{B}{$\dfrac{2\alpha}{\mathrm{GMr}_0^2}$}
\opt{C}{$\dfrac{\alpha}{\mathrm{GMr}_0^2}$}
\opt{D}{$\dfrac{3\alpha}{\mathrm{GMr}_0^2}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

{\footnotesize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{1pt}\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|l|l|}

 & \shortstack{Column-I\\(Velocity)} & & \shortstack{Column-II\\(Total Energy)} & & \shortstack{Column-III\\(Path)}\\
